# Chapter 14: Four Interviews, One Format, Zero Identical Rounds | Rostislav Borovikov · LinkedIn · 2026-09-07

**Rostislav Borovikov**: Rostislav Borovikov has held roles including Java Software Engineer at VADAROD, Java Software Engineer at InStock Technologies, and Java Software Engineer at IBA Group. Based in Minsk, Minsk, Belarus [BY].

---

Chapter 14: Four Interviews, One Format, Zero Identical Rounds

The final loop: four interviews, 60 minutes each. Every single round followed the exact same skeleton - 30 minutes of Leadership Principles, 30 minutes of a technical task. Yet, the technical halves felt completely different.

Before the loop, the recruiter shared the evaluation map. The core technical competencies spanned System Design, DSA, Logical & Maintainable Coding, Problem Solving, and Generative AI fluency. The LP focus was heavy on Earn Trust, Customer Obsession, Deliver Results, Ownership, Invent and Simplify, Bias for Action, and Insist on the Highest Standards.
Here is exactly how those four technical halves broke down (formats only, no specific tasks):

🔹 Round 1: Classic Algorithmic Task
This was an easy-level problem, the kind you have likely run into on LeetCode. I found the optimal solution quickly, which led straight into the real test: "What is the Big O of your solution?" Expect this question every single time. It is never enough to just make the code work - you have to know exactly how much that solution costs in time and memory.

🔹 Round 2: Multi-Stage Business Service
The goal here was to implement a service covering a multi-step business scenario. Once that was done, the interviewer threw a wrench in it: "Now add this functionality." From there, the conversation shifted straight into SOLID principles and how to make the design more robust. This round tests how easily your code bends before it breaks.

🔹 Round 3: System Design
This is the round where I made my biggest mistake of the entire interview process. It honestly deserves its own dedicated write-up - so I will save the breakdown for my next post.

🔹 Round 4: Data Structure & Behavior
I had to implement a custom data structure with specific functional requirements, then defend my architecture. We focused heavily on trade-offs and design choices. The interviewer was visibly satisfied, and the rest of the hour turned into a genuine, candid conversation about his actual work at Amazon. That final, informal chat taught me more about the company culture than any career page ever could.

💡 My biggest takeaway on the difficulty level:
Nothing here was overwhelmingly complex. Across the entire loop, the coding tasks sat comfortably at an easy-to-medium LeetCode level. The bar isn't raw, genius-level difficulty. The bar is how you reason, communicate, and defend your decisions under a ticking clock.
The tasks are intentionally sized for about 20 minutes. The remaining time - the discussion, the trade-offs, and the follow-up questions - is where you are actually being evaluated.

Up next: The System Design round. The one round I would completely redo if I could.

👨💻 [Amazon](https://linkedin.com/company/amazon) Interview Experience – Frontend Engineer(SDE-2) [Part 14]

Continuing my series on interview experiences, where I share the lessons, challenges, and takeaways from different stages of my journey.

💻 Online Assessment (OA)
The OA focused on coding and problem-solving, along with work-style/work-simulation assessments. The exact format can vary depending on the role and hiring cycle.

🏢 Interview Structure (4 Rounds)
The interview process evaluated candidates across:
DSA / Problem Solving
[Amazon](https://linkedin.com/company/amazon) Leadership Principles
React & Frontend fundamentals
Frontend System Design
AI Fluency

Round 1 – Technical: JavaScript, React, HTML/CSS & frontend fundamentals.
Round 2 – Technical: Frontend coding, problem-solving & JavaScript concepts.
Round 3 – System Design: Frontend architecture, scalability, performance & design decisions.
Round 4 (Bar Raiser) – Leadership Principles + technical discussion.

Some key highlights:
Strong emphasis on JavaScript fundamentals rather than only framework knowledge.
Expect practical frontend coding and problem-solving questions.
Frontend System Design becomes increasingly important at mid/senior levels.
Leadership Principles are evaluated throughout the process, not just in the Bar Raiser.
Be prepared to explain your technical decisions, trade-offs and real-world project experience.

# Amazon New Grad Software Engineer Interview Experience — AWS Offer After Four Onsite Rounds

Amazon· Software Engineer· Aug 2026

Timeline:

July 24: HR reached out on LinkedIn; I applied. July 31: OA. August 24: Survey. September 4: BOS onsite. September 10: Verbal offer.

Four back-to-back onsite rounds.

First round

The interviewer asked two behavioral questions: one about doing something outside my area of responsibility, and one about helping a peer who was struggling.

The coding question was similar to LeetCode 1152, but seemed a little easier: I only had to consider consecutive logs.

Second round

The bar raiser pressed hard on three Dive Deep questions and one about critical feedback, then left ten-plus minutes for my questions.

Third round

There was an interviewer and a shadow interviewer. The behavioral questions included a tight deadline and a time I hadn't finished by the deadline.

Thirty minutes for two coding problems: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters and Word Search II. Both were exactly the standard problems.

Fourth round

The hiring manager asked GenAI-related questions and wanted detailed examples, including examples of mistakes.

The coding question was to design a rate limiter. The prompt was vague and provided nothing; I had to clarify everything myself. After asking my questions, I used a deque for a sliding window. The interviewer kept asking what could replace the deque, and I couldn't answer. There were some other follow-ups too.

I originally thought my poor answers to the follow-ups in this round would be a problem, but they didn't seem to have much impact.

Published Sep 13, 2026

# Recently, I had the opportunity to go through the Amazon SDE interview loop, and I genuinely enjoyed how much the process challenged me. | Maria Preethi R · LinkedIn · 2026-09-02

**Maria Preethi R**: Software Engineer Intern at Foxen for 1 month with 5 years 4 months of total professional experience. Previous roles include AI ML engineer intern at Community Dreams Foundation, Digital philanthropy associate at University of Cincinnati Foundation, and Software Engineer at Dr. MCR HRD Institute of Telangana. Based in Columbus, Ohio Metropolitan Area [US].

---

Recently, I had the opportunity to go through the Amazon SDE interview loop, and I genuinely enjoyed how much the process challenged me.

It was a 4-round loop covering DSA problem solving, Low-Level Design/System Design, and Amazon Leadership Principles.

Two rounds focused on DSA questions in the LeetCode medium to medium-hard range, with patterns similar to Number of Islands and Search in Rotated Sorted Array.

One thing became clear quickly 😅 getting to a working solution is only the beginning.
Why this approach? Can you optimize it? What is the time and space complexity? What edge case could break it? What happens if the constraints change?

My earlier Microsoft interview experience taught me to clarify requirements, think aloud, discuss tradeoffs, and test edge cases instead of rushing straight into code. That definitely helped me approach this loop with more structure and confidence.

The Low-Level Design round was equally interesting. I had to take a real-world problem, identify the core objects and responsibilities, think through component relationships, extensibility, edge cases, and explain the tradeoffs behind my design decisions.

The Leadership Principles round went deep too. Ownership, Dive Deep, Deliver Results, ambiguity, mistakes, and decision making all came up through examples from my own work.

Amazon also taught me that a STAR story is never fully finished 😂
“Why?”
“What exactly did YOU do?”
“What would you do differently?”
…and suddenly you are five follow-up questions deeper.

I was informed that I successfully cleared the interview process, but the role unfortunately could not move forward because of headcount constraints. It was disappointing, but I’m grateful for the experience and the confidence it gave me.

A big thank you to the Amazon recruiting team, and the interviewers for a thoughtful and challenging experience.

#Amazon #SDE #SoftwareEngineering #DSA #SystemDesign #LeadershipPrinciples #CareerGrowth
